```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
                      out.width = "100%", dpi = 130)

# This vignette PLOTS precomputed benchmark results shipped with the package; it
# runs no model fits, so it builds fast and needs no benchmark competitors at
# build time. The live study is inst/benchmark/run_benchmark.R.
.viz_pkgs <- c("ggplot2", "scales", "patchwork", "dplyr", "tidyr")
.has_data <- nzchar(system.file("extdata/benchmark_results.rds",
                                package = "fastsimplexreg"))
has_viz <- .has_data &&
  all(vapply(.viz_pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))

if (has_viz) {
  results_path <- system.file("extdata", package = "fastsimplexreg")
  source(system.file("benchmark", "viz_figures.R", package = "fastsimplexreg"))
  results <- readRDS(file.path(results_path, "benchmark_results.rds"))
  coefs <- readRDS(file.path(results_path, "benchmark_coefs.rds"))
  # Read explicitly: `meta` used to arrive only as a side effect of source()ing
  # viz_figures.R, so any refactor there broke this vignette silently.
  meta <- readRDS(file.path(results_path, "benchmark_meta.rds"))
}
```

## What this compares, and how to read it

`fastsimplexreg` aims to be a fast, modern implementation of **simplex regression**
for proportions in $(0, 1)$. This article benchmarks it against two packages for
bounded responses, `betareg` (on CRAN) and `simplexreg` (archived on CRAN), and is
explicit about what each comparison does and does not prove:

* **vs [`simplexreg`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=simplexreg)** (archived
  on CRAN) — both packages fit a simplex model, so they can be compared on
  **both accuracy and speed**. Sections 1 and 4 show where the estimates agree and
  where they do not.
* **vs [`betareg`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=betareg)** — the *beta*
  distribution, a different model. This is a fair **speed / capability** comparator
  (both fit mean-and-dispersion regressions for $(0,1)$ data) but **not** an
  accuracy comparator, because the likelihoods differ.
* **Mixed models** — there is *no* CRAN package that fits a simplex mixed model, so
  `fastsimplexregmixed()` is benchmarked on its own scaling.

A deliberate omission: we **never** compare log-likelihoods across packages. On the
very same fit where the coefficients agree to seven digits, the reported `logLik`
values differ in sign and magnitude, because the packages use different additive
conventions (and `betareg` is a different family). Accuracy is judged through
coefficient agreement.

```{r methods-note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (has_viz) {
  # Print "OpenBLAS 0.3.26" rather than the library path.
  blas_label <- function(path) {
    m <- regmatches(path, regexec("libopenblas[a-z]*-r([0-9.]*[0-9])\\.so", path))[[1]]
    if (length(m) == 2L) paste("OpenBLAS", m[2]) else basename(path)
  }
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0("*All results are precomputed with `fastsimplexreg` %s, `simplexreg` %s ",
           "and `betareg` %s (%s, %s; %d cores; seed %s; run on %s). ",
           "They have not been re-run for later versions of `fastsimplexreg`. ",
           "Each package receives the identical data per cell; ",
           "`fastsimplexreg` is timed single-core and at 4 threads, and the ",
           "single-core number is always shown.*\n"),
    meta$versions$fastsimplexreg, meta$versions$simplexreg,
    meta$versions$betareg, meta$r_version, blas_label(meta$blas), meta$n_cores,
    meta$seed,
    substr(meta$date, 1, 10)))
}
```

## 1. Accuracy on simulated data

Fitting the identical simplex model (logit mean with two covariates, log dispersion
with one) on simulated data, `fastsimplexreg` and `simplexreg` return the same
estimates. The largest coefficient difference is 7.8e-7 (at $n = 500$) and it
*shrinks* as $n$ grows, to 1.1e-9 at $n = 8000$.

```{r tab-accuracy, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Built from the shipped results rather than hard-coded, so the table can never
# drift away from the figures below when the benchmark is re-run.
if (has_viz) {
  acc <- results[results$scenario == "accuracy", ]
  tm <- stats::aggregate(time_sec ~ package + n, data = acc, FUN = stats::median)
  wide <- stats::reshape(tm, idvar = "n", timevar = "package", direction = "wide")
  fs <- wide[["time_sec.fastsimplexreg"]]
  sr <- wide[["time_sec.simplexreg"]]
  cd <- vapply(wide$n, function(nn) {
    z <- coefs[coefs$scenario == "accuracy" & coefs$n == nn, ]
    a <- z$estimate[z$package == "fastsimplexreg"]
    b <- z$estimate[z$package == "simplexreg"]
    if (length(a) && length(a) == length(b)) max(abs(a - b)) else NA_real_
  }, numeric(1))
  cat("| $n$ | max &#124;coef diff&#124; | fastsimplexreg | simplexreg | speed-up |\n")
  cat("|----:|:------------:|:--------------:|:----------:|:--------:|\n")
  for (i in order(wide$n)) {
    cat(sprintf("| %d | %.1e | %.4f s | %.4f s | %.1f&times; |\n",
                wide$n[i], cd[i], fs[i], sr[i], sr[i] / fs[i]))
  }
}
```

```{r fig-accuracy, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.6}
fig_accuracy()
```

## 2. Scaling: the workhorse comparison

The central question — how does fit time grow with the sample size? Every package
is fed the same $(0,1)$ data and the same mean-and-dispersion model, for
$n = 200$ up to $500{,}000$.

```{r fig-scaling, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5}
fig_scaling()
```

| $n$     | fast (1t) | fast (4t) | simplexreg | betareg | simplexreg / fast | betareg / fast |
|--------:|:---------:|:---------:|:----------:|:-------:|:-----------------:|:--------------:|
| 200     | 0.0020 | 0.0020 | 0.0150 | 0.0070 | 7.5&times;  | 3.5&times;  |
| 1000    | 0.0050 | 0.0030 | 0.0630 | 0.0220 | 12.6&times; | 4.4&times;  |
| 5000    | 0.0360 | 0.5160 | 0.4830 | 0.0945 | 13.4&times; | 2.6&times;  |
| 20000   | 0.1490 | 0.5970 | 1.0600 | 0.3600 | 7.1&times;  | 2.4&times;  |
| 100000  | 0.8370 | 1.4480 | 4.4300 | 1.9540 | 5.3&times;  | 2.3&times;  |
| 500000  | 17.28  | 3.2475 | 20.94  | 8.6075 | 1.2&times;  | 0.5&times;  |

With `fastsimplexreg` 0.2.1 at a single thread and a logit link, the fit is
**5.3–13.4&times; faster than `simplexreg`** and
**2.3–4.4&times; faster than `betareg`** for $n$ up to $10^5$. At
$n = 5\times10^5$ the single-thread advantage is much smaller: **1.2&times;**
over `simplexreg`, and `fastsimplexreg` took about twice as long as `betareg`.
The scaling is
near-linear up to $10^5$ (log-log slope $\approx 1.0$); the competitors have
slightly lower slopes (about 0.9) but larger constant factors.

```{r fig-speedup, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6}
fig_speedup()
```

Two points to note. First, **multithreading is a scale-up story, not a free
win**: at $n = 5000$, $20000$ and $10^5$ four threads are *slower* than one
(0.52 s against 0.04 s, 0.60 s against 0.15 s, and 1.45 s against 0.84 s), and
the payoff appears at large scale (at $n = 5\times10^5$ the
4-thread run, 3.25 s, is the fastest of all four). Version 0.2.1 computed the
linear predictors through BLAS and later versions do not (see `NEWS.md`), so
the threaded timings here may not carry over to them.
Second, the **single-thread $n = 5\times10^5$ cell** took 17.3 s against 0.84 s
at $n = 10^5$ (21 times longer for 5 times the data, two repetitions), and we
draw no advantage from it — only the 4-thread result there supports a claim.

## 3. All four mean links

`fastsimplexreg` supports `logit`, `probit`, `cloglog` and `neglog` mean links.
At $n = 3000$ every fit converges in both packages, and `fastsimplexreg` is
consistently faster.

```{r fig-links, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 4.4}
fig_links()
```

## 4. Real data

On the three standard datasets from `betareg` — `GasolineYield`, `ReadingSkills`
and `FoodExpenditure` — all three packages fit a constant-dispersion model
successfully, and `fastsimplexreg` is at least as fast as both references. The
`fastsimplexreg` and `simplexreg` fitted means have correlation 1.00 on every
dataset and the mean coefficients agree, but the two packages do **not** return
the same dispersion intercept:

```{r tab-realdata, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Built from the shipped coefficients, like the accuracy table above. n is the
# sample size and p the number of mean coefficients of the fitted model.
if (has_viz) {
  rd <- coefs[coefs$scenario == "realdata" &
                coefs$package %in% c("fastsimplexreg", "simplexreg"), ]
  cat("| data set | $n$ | $p$ | max &#124;mean coef diff&#124; | dispersion intercept, fastsimplexreg | dispersion intercept, simplexreg | simplexreg &minus; fastsimplexreg | $\\log\\{n/(n-p)\\}$ |\n")
  cat("|:---------|:--:|:--:|:------------:|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|\n")
  for (ds in c("GasolineYield", "ReadingSkills", "FoodExpenditure")) {
    z <- rd[rd$dataset == ds, ]
    est <- function(pk, tm) z$estimate[z$package == pk & z$term == tm]
    mt <- unique(z$term[grepl("^mean:", z$term)])
    md <- max(abs(vapply(mt, function(tm) est("fastsimplexreg", tm) -
                                         est("simplexreg", tm), numeric(1))))
    a <- est("fastsimplexreg", "disp:(Intercept)")
    b <- est("simplexreg", "disp:(Intercept)")
    n <- z$n[1L]
    p <- length(mt)
    cat(sprintf("| %s | %d | %d | %.1e | %.3f | %.3f | %.4f | %.4f |\n",
                ds, n, p, md, a, b, b - a, log(n / (n - p))))
  }
}
```

The dispersion intercepts are on the log scale. The gap equals
$\log\{n/(n-p)\}$, with $p$ the number of mean coefficients, so `simplexreg`
appears to rescale the maximum-likelihood dispersion by $n/(n-p)$ (deviance over
residual degrees of freedom). `simplexreg` is archived on CRAN and is not
installed here, so its code was not read and it was not re-run for this article.
Identical estimates are therefore shown only on the simulated data of Section 1,
where the dispersion depends on a covariate and the estimates agree.

```{r fig-realdata, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6}
fig_realdata()
```

These datasets are tiny ($n \le 44$) with millisecond fit times, so the real-data
speed-ups are directionally consistent rather than precise multipliers.

## 5. The mixed model — where nothing else exists

No CRAN package fits a simplex mixed model, so this shows `fastsimplexregmixed()`
scaling on its own: a random-intercept model with 8 observations per cluster,
across $J \in \{50, 200, 1000\}$ clusters and $\texttt{nAGQ} \in \{1, 7, 15\}$.

```{r fig-mixed, echo = FALSE, eval = has_viz, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.6}
fig_mixed()
```

The cost is **linear in the number of clusters** (going from 50 to 1000 clusters —
8000 observations — costs about 4 s single-threaded), **higher-order quadrature is
nearly free** (raising `nAGQ` from 7 to 15 adds only a few percent), and four
threads give a steady **~2&times;** speed-up. The one non-converged cell
($J = 1000$, `nAGQ = 1`) is the expected limitation of the crude Laplace
approximation at a large cluster count; `nAGQ >= 7` converges cleanly and is only
marginally more expensive — the practical recommendation is to use `nAGQ >= 7` for
large $J$.

## Bottom line

* **vs `simplexreg`** (`fastsimplexreg` 0.2.1, single thread): the same
  estimates on simulated data (max coefficient difference $7.8\times10^{-7}$),
  **5.3–13.4&times; faster** for $n$ up to $10^5$ (logit link) and 1.2&times;
  at $n = 5\times10^5$. On the real data sets the fitted means agree but the
  dispersion intercepts differ by 0.065–0.082, which equals $\log\{n/(n-p)\}$
  (Section 4).
* **vs `betareg`** (a different, beta model; speed only): **2.3–4.4&times;
  faster** single-thread for $n$ up to $10^5$ (logit link); at
  $n = 5\times10^5$ `fastsimplexreg` took about twice as long.
* **Mixed model:** the only tractable simplex GLMM available, linear in clusters,
  with nearly-free higher-order quadrature.

## Reproducing the benchmark

The figures above are rendered from precomputed results shipped with the package
(`system.file("extdata", package = "fastsimplexreg")`). The full, self-contained
study that generated them is installed with the package:

```{r repro, eval = FALSE}
# The complete benchmark (fits simplexreg / betareg / fastsimplexreg across every
# scenario) and the plotting code:
file.edit(system.file("benchmark", "run_benchmark.R", package = "fastsimplexreg"))
file.edit(system.file("benchmark", "viz_figures.R",  package = "fastsimplexreg"))

# Re-run end to end (requires betareg and simplexreg; simplexreg is archived on
# CRAN and must be installed from the CRAN archive):
source(system.file("benchmark", "run_benchmark.R", package = "fastsimplexreg"))
```

Timings depend on hardware and the BLAS in use; the shipped results were measured
on a 24-core machine with a multi-threaded OpenBLAS, which is exactly why the
single-thread numbers are reported alongside the threaded ones.
